objectives: LO 5.1.1: Compare ways to own investment real estate, value it with NOI and cap rates, and know how it is taxed
LO 5.2.1: Recognize option types and positions, payoffs, intrinsic/time value, pricing-model inputs and option taxation
LO 5.2.2: Choose option strategies for speculation, income and hedging (covered calls, protective puts, collars, straddles)
LO 5.3.1: Explain futures terms, margin and marking to market, short vs. long hedges, and 60/40 taxation
LO 5.4.1: Weigh collectibles, gold and natural resources, including liquidity and the 28% collectibles rate
LO 5.5.1: Assess the risks and benefits of foreign securities, market types, fund choices and ADRs
LO 5.5.2: Measure how exchange rate moves change a foreign investment's return in dollars
synthesis: Module 5 adds the tools that sit beside stocks and bonds: real assets and foreign securities widen diversification because they move differently from U.S. financial assets, while options and futures let a client transfer or shape risk. In planning, these show up as REIT income sleeves, collars on concentrated stock, index puts or futures as portfolio insurance, and international funds whose currency exposure must be explained. Each carries its own liquidity, leverage and tax rules that feed directly into asset allocation and tax planning.

example.title: Collar on a concentrated position
example.html:
Rina owns 1,000 shares bought at $20, now $60. She buys 10 puts with a $55 strike at $2.40 and writes 10 calls with a $70 strike at $2.40.

  • Net premium: $2,400 received − $2,400 paid = $0 (zero-cost collar)
  • Floor: if the stock falls to $40, she can sell at $55 → value protected at $55,000
  • Ceiling: above $70 the shares are called away at $70 → value capped at $70,000
  • Range kept until expiration: $55,000 to $70,000, versus $60,000 today

keyNumbers: NOI excludes depreciation and debt service
Distribute ≥90% of net earnings; ≥75% of gross income from real estate (2026 edition figures)
Multiply per-share premiums and payoffs by 100
Call BE = strike + premium; put BE = strike − premium
Applies to buyer and writer alike
Margin call restores the initial level
Regardless of holding period (2026 edition figure)
Possible advisor cap in a diversified portfolio
mustKnow: Max gain/loss for all four option positions: only the long call (gain) and naked short call (loss) are unlimited
Intrinsic value: call = stock − strike, put = strike − stock, never below zero; time value = premium − intrinsic
Black-Scholes: every input raises call value except the exercise price
Short hedge = own the asset, sell futures; long hedge = need the asset, buy futures
REIT income is portfolio income; RELPs fall under passive activity rules
A U.S. owner of foreign securities wants the dollar to fall during the holding period; ADRs keep currency risk
traps: Subtracting mortgage interest or depreciation when computing NOI
Calling a long put's gain unlimited (it is strike − premium)
Restoring a futures account only to maintenance margin
Hedging a short sale with puts instead of calls
Choosing a global fund to diversify away from U.S. holdings
tips: Write the four-position payoff table from memory before any option question
For currency questions, first restate the quote as foreign units per $1, then divide to get dollars
Hedges always take the position opposite the cash exposure
